3.text: nose is easily frost-bitten “short of souls” (uviriˊtkɪlin), meaning that some part

4.text: of his vital force must have left his body unawares. The “limb-souls” stay

5.text: on the spot where they were lost. A shaman, however, can call them to

6.text: himself, and they become his “assistant spirits” (yaˊnřa-kaˊlat). The “souls”

7.text: are very small. When passing by, they produce a sound like the humming

8.text: of a bee or the droning of a beetle.

9.text: One or all of the “souls” of the whole person may be stolen by the keˊlet,

10.text: then the man becomes sick, and finally dies. The shaman can find and

11.text: restore a missing “soul.” The “soul,” when found by a shaman, often

12.text: assumes the shape of a black beetle. When put on the body of the patient,

13.text: it will crawl all over his head, trying to find a hole into which to slip.

14.text: Then the shaman will open the skull, and put the beetle in its proper place.

15.text: The beetle may enter through the mouth, the armpit, the intestines, the toes

17.text: If the shaman fails to find the “soul,” he can blow into the person a

18.text: part of his own spirit to become a “soul;” or he may give him one of his

20.text: Keˊlet, when getting possession of a “soul,” often take it to their world

21.text: and pinion its hands, or bind all its limbs separately with strong bands. Then

22.text: they put it behind the lamp, in the place where many small things are

23.text: usually kept. In the tale of “The Scabby Shaman,” the female keˊlᴇ-bird,

24.text: after having brought home the “soul” of Rɪˊntew, secures it with iron bands,

25.text: puts it behind the lamp, and feeds it with choicest meat and tallow in order

26.text: to fatten it and make it fit to be eaten.

27.text: In another tale, a keˊlᴇ forces a stolen “soul” to watch his lamp and

28.text: trim it; in still another, he uses it as a trimming-stick.

29.text: “Souls” are liable to injury even from material weapons. I know of a

30.text: case where a man struck his wife with a firebrand. The woman died in two

31.text: days. The relatives, after ripping up and investigating the dead body, said

32.text: that none of her vital organs were injured, but that probably the man

33.text: wounded her “souls” with the blow. Keˊlet, also, have “souls” of their own,

34.text: which may be lost, or spirited away by shamans.

40.text: The largest dwell in the larynx and in the left side, and are tiny men, about the size of a sparrow. The

41.text: other souls dwell in other parts of the body, and are of the size of a finger-joint. If one of them is taken

42.text: away, the member to which it belongs sickens (Holm, Meddelelser om Grønland, Part X, p. 112, cited
